utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, ma'am. Mr. Brdjanin, can you follow the proceedings in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, and good morning to you. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Julian Nicholls with Denise Gustin, and again with us today is Mr. Dominic Raab, who is a legal advisor to the British Embassy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Nicholls. Good morning to you, and good morning to you, Mr. Raab.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Appearances for Mr. Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I'm John Ackerman. I'm here with David Cunningham and Aleksandar Vujic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Ackerman, and good morning. First thing, my apologies and those of the Tribunal for starting with almost a half an hour's delay. The reason is that we had shifted the sitting from the afternoon to the morning. It was done rather late in the day. And apparently something went wrong in the chain of communications, and we had one section of the Trial Chamber and not serviced in time this morning due to this minor fault, which I -- which I can't blame on anyone in particular. So my apologies. My apologies to you too, sir. And perhaps we can start straight away. Usher, could you please hand the solemn declaration to the witness. And proceed. Tough.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You will be cross-examined today, as you know, and tomorrow, by Mr. Ackerman, who is lead counsel for Mr. Brdjanin. Thank you, Mr. Brown.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, before I begin, last week I had submitted two Defence exhibits, DB150 and DB152. Apparently they were not properly tendered, and so I have returned them to the Registrar this morning and asked that they be admitted. I don't think they were used during the testimony, but they will be in future testimony. So before I lose them, I'd submit them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I thank you, Mr. Ackerman. We'll stay in open session all the time, Mr. Nicholls, no?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, it depends, Your Honour. As -- as you had the order regarding this witness, background information of a certain type will need to be in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. You will keep an open eye on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. And I think Mr. Ackerman as well knows the areas which ought to be in private, and I trust him on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Let's proceed. Thank you. Cross-examined by Mr. Ackerman:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And -- I think you go ahead, Mr. Ackerman. Mr. Nicholls will draw your attention if there is anything --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I really don't want to say something that I shouldn't have said, and I think, I think that the area I got to stay away from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, more or less -- more or less it was that, yes. More or less it was that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Cross-examined by Mr. Ackerman:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to begin by discussing a little bit with you the question of -- of how you see your role as a military expert in this case. I -- if one just looks at your report, it seems to me that there are a couple of possibilities. And please feel free to disagree with me if I'm wrong about any of this. It seems to me that one -- one possibility that -- that you had as you approached this was to -- to consult all the documents that were selected and present to this Trial Chamber a report which in every way possible would favour the position of the Prosecution as set out in the indictment. Or, on the other hand, what you could have done was looked at the selected documents and tried to provide this Trial Chamber with an honest assessment of what you believe those documents -- the conclusions you believe could be drawn from those documents. Can you tell us which of those, if either, was the way you approached this process, this task.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: The latter, I would argue. I was given the task and to the best of my ability I searched through the documents on the databases of the OTP and attempted where I could to analyse and articulate what I believed these documents to tell me and to say. So I would argue it was the latter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what you tried to present to this Trial Chamber, what you intended to present to this Trial Chamber, was an honest assessment of -- of what could be logically concluded from the contents of these documents. Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so. Obviously there -- I've articulated certain limitations with -- with the report. I clearly wouldn't have seen and haven't seen every single document in the holding of the OTP. But based on the documents I was able to see and review, I -- I would argue that I've tried to be as -- as honest and -- as I can with the -- with the material available to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I take it that --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Excuse me, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] One moment, Mr. Ackerman. Mr. Nicholls, yes,.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, can we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's go into private session, for a while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What I want to make sure also is, Madam Registrar, when someone asks for transcripts of this session, what is said in private session, does it show up or not?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: If it's for the release to the public, it will be redacted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I assume that prior to undertaking this task --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think what I want to do is take us back into private session and just get through all of this preliminary stuff that way, just so I don't run any more risks here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Anything against, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No. I think that's a good idea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Let's go into private session again for a while, until we thrash this initial part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to first begin discussing with you the conceded limitations of the report that you have given to this Trial Chamber. And for that I'd ask you to look at page 4 of your report, under the heading "Introduction." I assume you have your report with you.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In paragraph 3, on that page, you -- you tell us this: "This report is based exclusively on an analysis of selected military, police, political, and other related documentary material in the possession of the Office of the Prosecutor of the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia and is not an exhaustive analysis of all aspects of events in the Bosanska Krajina area between 1991-1992." Correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You used the word "selected," "analysis of selected" documentary material. Who performed the selection?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: I selected the documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So no one selected them for you. You were given access to the Prosecutor's document database, apparently, and selected what you thought was relevant.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. There may have been one or two instances where, say, colleagues within the team that I work in may have flagged up some documents that they thought I might have been interested in, but the documents were selected by me from the database, as you state.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in order to do that in any kind of a logical way, I take it you had to familiarise yourself with the indictment in this case to be able to do that.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: I was, of course, familiar with the indictment. However, it wasn't in itself a document that I made constant reference to or read. I was aware of it and I was aware of the general content of it, but it wasn't necessarily something that structured the report as it was written. Clearly there was overlaps and there was areas, and I was aware of the general areas of interest from the indictment, but it wasn't sitting on my desk open every day for me to refer to. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you were certainly aware of the Prosecutor's theory of the case, of this case, and the contentions of the Prosecutor as contained in the indictment, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes, in general terms. I'm not a lawyer, so clearly some of the nuances and minutiae I'm not aware of, but I, of course, am aware from the indictment of the case, so yes. But I'm -- as I say, I'm not a lawyer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please understand I'm not suggesting there's anything wrong with you being familiar with the indictment. I don't know how you would have written a report if you weren't. So please don't take anything I'm saying to you to be any kind of a criticism. Did you assist in any way in drafting the indictment?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: I was asked for comments at certain stages during the indictment process on aspects the lawyers were discussing or were writing, but I wasn't involved per se in the writing of the indictment, but I was asked for comments or whether there was documentation, certainly military documentation, that could assist certain aspects. So yes, I was in that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: When did you join the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I joined in 1998, in August 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that in looking at specific documents and considering specific documents that -- that you might have found useful that many of them tend to be ambiguous and capable of more than one interpretation?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: That -- that is the case in -- in some of them, yes. I would say that -- that certainly if you take some documents in isolation or individually there can be an ambiguity. I'm not sure what you mean by "many," if you mean them all or a significant percentage, but, you know, some documents do have a certain ambiguity, depending on what they are.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I suggest that where there was -- a document is capable of more than one interpretation, that almost invariably you chose the interpretation most favourable to the Prosecutor's position. Didn't you?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: I wouldn't necessarily agree with that, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever make any inquiry of the Defence team in this case as to whether there were any documents that you should consider in drafting this report for the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many times would you say that you sat in on interviews with potential witnesses in this case as part of the team that was interviewing a witness?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: I couldn't -- I couldn't remember how many. I have sat in on a number of interviews, but I cannot put a figure on it. It's -- it isn't that many, actually. Maybe at most a dozen. But I'm a little unclear as to how many exactly it would be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you were sitting in on the interviews of potential witnesses in this case, you were there as part of the Prosecutor's investigative team, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes, I clearly worked for the Office of the Prosecutor, and the team that I work in is a part of the investigation division of the Office of the Prosecutor. When I was asked to assist in those interviews, it was because I had acquired some expertise certainly in some of the military documentation and they wanted me to assist them in that manner. So it was an assisting role for the benefit of the Office of the Prosecutor and clearly I am -- I work for the Office of the Prosecutor, so ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, that kind of takes us back to the very beginning. You told us that your role with regard to this report was to look at the documents and to give the Chamber a completely honest assessment of what you believe these documents show. But other times you found yourself in the role of a member of the Prosecutor's investigating team, basically as a -- as a prosecutorial advocate. And what I'm wondering is how are we to know when you are a prosecutorial advocate and when you are --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The witness never characterised himself as a "prosecutorial advocate," which is what is being implied here by Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, objection sustained, Mr. Ackerman. Please suggest something else to the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would say a member of the prosecutorial team --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How would we know when you are when you are this impartial, unbiased trying to give an honest assessment of the documents expert and when you are a member of a prosecutorial investigative team trying to further the case of the Prosecution? How can we tell when you're wearing -- which hat you're wearing?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: I don't necessarily subscribe to the view that the two are somehow exclusive. I'm an analysis who works for the Office of the Prosecutor. I've been involved in analytical work all my career. I've always taken the view that -- that it is as my job as an analyst to review material that I see and give an objective view of that material, whether that helps or hinders anybody. This wasn't unusual when I was in the military either. All I can say is that -- that as my role as an analyst within the Office of the Prosecutor to look at material that I see, to review it objectively, and to attempt to place some context and meaning behind it in a -- a common-sense and hopefully a rational manner. And when I was asked in those other tasks that you -- you mentioned, that I would give the same answer as if I was having to write a report on it. So all I can say is that I'm -- I'm an analyst who attempts to look at the material and give an objective view on it, whether it's for whatever purpose.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's -- let's start looking at some specific instances then. Turn to page 16 of your report, paragraph 1.17, please. Tell me when you're there.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: I'm there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said this: "Although it is likely that some of the attempts at the local level were genuine in their desire to reduce the ethnic division, the objective of the 5th Corps was again to assist in keeping Bosnia and Herzegovina within Yugoslavia and that the JNA should not be withdrawn from Bosnia and Herzegovina at any price." Now, that's what you wrote. You're telling the Trial Chamber by that sentence that -- that the 5th Corps objective was to keep Bosnia within Yugoslavia and to keep the JNA from being withdrawn. Correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes. And I -- I believe the footnote makes a reference to that -- that type of statement, that --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And I now want you to look at the document DB195, please. I believe this is the document that you refer to in the footnote, the translation ERN 01101236, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please find in there what you believe supports that sentence that we just read.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: On page 2, in the paragraph entitled "State of morale," it has the line: "All unanimously believe that withdrawal of the JNA from BH should not be allowed at any price. Telegrams by various associations of citizens are arriving in the corps command, expressing support for the JNA and requesting that it does not withdraw from BH." That -- that is, in terms of the sentence at 1.17, the reference that I hinted there. The other aspects about ethnic tension I believe are from other documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But that's it? That's what you -- that's what you say supports that sentence?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First of all, that's a section of the document under the heading "State of morale," isn't it?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it deals with basically what someone is hearing in the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. grumbling among officers and troops, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: I'm not sure you can draw that conclusion from that section. The state of morale component of the daily combat report was usually a section that would give the political flavour from the JNA's perspective, was usually written by the assistant commander for morale of the corps, and usually, as I say, had -- as a -- had the political message that was being disseminated either up the chain or down to the units on the ground.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you've looked at hundreds of these reports, and all of the combat reports or virtually all of them have a section called "morale," or "State of morale," and almost invariably they deal with what the writer of that is hearing from the soldiers on the ground, basically, what are their -- how are they feeling, what are their attitudes, and so forth. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is exactly the same question which he -- the witness has just answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls. Objection sustained. You are asking the same question again, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Judge, I sure don't think so. But if that's your position, I'll go at it a little differently.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When it says there in the second paragraph: "All unanimously believe," what the writer is referring to is conversations with officers and troops, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes, you could probably draw that -- that conclusion, that it's from the JNA themselves and based probably on the sentence previously.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That -- that is not a section of the report that sets out JNA policy or 5th Corps policy, is it?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Well, this is a report which is going to the highest level of command or the -- the superior command of the 5th Corps, and it's not the only document that I've seen whereby in that early period, in the first few months of 1992, the JNA were making references that Yugoslavia should be preserved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please answer my question. This is not a section of the report that sets out 5th Corps or JNA policy. It's just talking about the feelings of the troops, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Well, I -- I can't say whether it's -- it's a document written by General Talic to the corps -- to the 2nd Military District in a section that usually deals with the political context, and he makes no reference in here that he disagrees with this -- this particular view. And my conclusion is that if it's going up there, it's -- it's something that -- that is agreed with. You're right. It doesn't specifically say "The JNA 5th Corps's policy is X,".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: But from this and other documents I would argue that the JNA 5th Corps were keen to ensure that Yugoslavia was preserved and that Bosnia was a component of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You could argue that, but what you say to the Chamber in your conclusion in this report is that this was an objective of the 5th Corps, and I put to you that nowhere in that document can you find that it was an objective of the 5th Corps to do what you say. Now, it may have been somewhere, but it's not in that document. And that's the document you refer the Chamber to. And it's not even an exhibit in the case until today. So the Chamber could have believed that there was a document saying that the 5th Corps's objective was to do this and not have even been able to check it because it wasn't an exhibit. That's my concern.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's an argument. It's not a question, and it's totally inappropriate to put that to the witness about which exhibits are in or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. It's a perfectly legitimate question, which I'm allowing and asking the witness to answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And don't you think that was a bit reckless to do it that way? It seems to me it's misleading to the Chamber. Isn't it?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: I hope -- it wasn't misleading to the Chamber. Maybe I could have put in three or four other footnote references that would bear out my view that it was an objective for the 5th Corps in line with the JNA policy to maintain Bosnia and Herzegovina within Yugoslavia

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, we talked a little earlier about your training and your learning to write reports and footnotes, and one of the things you learned was the footnotes should support your conclusions. And this one doesn't, does it?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Well, I would argue that it does.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's move on. I'd like to go to 1.25, on page 20. About halfway through that paragraph you write this sentence: "Additionally, there is evidence that Serb paramilitary units were also given direct authorisation by the 5th Corps to participate in combat operations in Western Slavonia. One of the clearest examples of this is related to a paramilitary group from Prnjavor area, headed by Veljko Milankovic." What other paramilitary units in April of 1992, which is what we're talking about here, during that time, were given direct authorisation by the 5th Corps to so participate?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Cigo's group from Prijedor, which was a component of the 43rd Motorised Brigade, Zolja's group, which was also a component of the 43rd Motorised Brigade, which operated in Western Slavonia; Zoran Karlica's group, which was an assault detachment 43rd Motorised Brigade, which operated in Western Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which was the first one, the one from Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Cigo's group, I think he said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Your Honour. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How do you spell it?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: C-i-g-o.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Any others?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: I'm unsure of other ones that spring to mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And we're -- are you restricting your questions only, and is the witness restricting his answers only to the area of Western Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, this paragraph specifically refers to activities in Western Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I just wanted to make that clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let's go now to 1.33, on page 22.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in that paragraph, you're talking about a particular meeting, that being apparently the extraordinary session of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, 28 April 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that paragraph, 1.33, you tell the Chamber this: "The meeting was not attended by members of the corps staff, despite there being calls for them to be present. Although, Veljko Milankovic, the paramilitary leader from Prnjavor, did speak. The assembly also endorsed a call from Nenad Stevandic, the head of the Serbian Sokol Society in Banja Luka, that roads be blocked if JNA units really did decide to withdraw from the Bosanska Krajina." I notice there's no cite to that paragraph. Did you get that information from the article in Glas that you cited in the previous paragraph?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. 1.34 says this: "The SOS had mounted blockades in Banja Luka in part to halt the withdrawal of JNA units from the area." And I think what you mean to tell us there is that the SOS was part of the effort to keep the JNA from departing and that was part of why the blockades were set up by the SOS in Banja Luka. Is that a fair characterisation of what you're trying to tell the Chamber there?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes. I think maybe as some context I believe that a few days prior to that there had been the declaration of the new FRY constitution, which indicated that only Serbia and Montenegro would be part of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and I believe that that had caused some consternation in the Krajina and Banja Luka that potentially the next Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. stage would be that the JNA were going to have to withdraw from Bosnia because Bosnia was no longer part of the FRY, and that potentially as a result of that declaration the extraordinary -- amongst other things, the extraordinary session was -- was held and that speakers at that session voiced this view that the JNA must not leave. Furthermore, the blockade at the end of April, highlighted here by the SOS, again may well have been a visible expression that, you know, we must not allow the JNA to depart. There had been an earlier blockade by the SOS in early April, which I believe was for their -- their stated aims were not that the JNA should leave. But I have to check that again. So there was context behind, I think, both that meeting and potentially the actions of the SOS on the second blockade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Well, I would argue -- I'm not sure if it had been decided that the JNA were going to physically leave, as opposed to this transition that occurred later on whereby JNA forces were in essence transformed into the VRS. What I think is some context behind this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let me just remind us all exactly what you wrote: "The Serbian defence forces who had in fact mounted blockades in Banja Luka in part to halt the withdrawal of JNA units from the area." And the footnote that you document -- you cite to in the football is Exhibit P1470. I'd like you now to look at that document and just tell the Chamber where in there it says that the Serbian defence forces mounted blockades in part to halt withdrawal of JNA units from the area. Just find that in the document for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If we could have it on the ELMO, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I might be able to help you if you look at paragraph 3, "Situation on the ground." My assumption is that you're basing that on what appears there in that first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes, I -- I think that is where I'm referencing that. In the second part of that paragraph, it makes mention of the education centre, which was based in Banja Luka and was a federal -- or a JNA asset, as opposed to a corps asset. And the Kosmos military complex and -- which again was a -- a JNA-wide military complex, as opposed to being a 5th Corps asset. So there -- there had been some potential relocation or discussion about potential relocation of those federal-level assets, and it does also make mention of the SOS barricading the exits from Banja Luka, prohibiting departure. So that is where I draw that, from there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you're talking about a -- a few guys with red berets and automatic weapons blocking the JNA with tanks and artillery and machine-guns and -- and very heavy weaponry. How -- how do you propose they were able to do that? How could they stop one of the -- one of the most well-equipped armies in Europe? That doesn't make any sense to us -- to me.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: I'm not sure I can necessarily add much that would drift into some element of speculation. I can't say if it was a few guys in red berets. But even if it was a relatively small -- smallish force, in comparison to the 5th Corps, which clearly would have been, I can only speculate that the 5th Corps themselves were not necessarily willing to move out or to -- to take on this particular paramilitary group. Maybe there was a commonality of view between the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And just to be clear, for the record as well, the paragraph itself does not state the assertion that Mr. Ackerman has just put to the witness. The paragraph does not state that a few guys in red berets were able to prevent the entire JNA from leaving. That is not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's true; it doesn't. But I think both you and Mr. Ackerman and us and certainly the witness knew more or less what -- what we are talking about. I mean, what I don't agree with is the conclusion that Mr. Ackerman was trying to suggest, because what is obviously is that the act of the SOS brought matters to a head and then decisions were taken. And this is how I understand you to be answering the question; once the matter was brought to a head, it was up to the JNA units to decide what to do. Are you of the opinion that they couldn't have faced the SOS and if they didn't face the SOS, how come they decided not to face the SOS? What's your answer to that? And more or less, we'll cover the territory that Mr. Ackerman was trying to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can only maybe draw your attention to the line in the paragraph that says "Problems were solved in cooperation with the Banja Luka Crisis Staff," in that the JNA had no intention of taking on in a military capacity this particular paramilitary group. Because, to be truthful, I would have thought the 5th Corps would have quite easily managed to take on such a paramilitary group. But the matter was dealt with in -- in some element of cooperation and negotiation. And I can only draw the conclusion that it was not necessarily in the interest of the JNA 5th Corps either to withdraw, and hence my comment about some element of commonality of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Does that satisfy your question, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I have a follow-up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The other possibility, of course, is that the -- the JNA was not excited about engaging in combat activities in the streets of Banja Luka because of the endanger -- the danger that would bring to the innocent civilians living there -- hoped that it could be solved, as you say, in cooperation with the Banja Luka Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Well, that is a potential. Clearly it might not necessarily have been in the interests of the 5th Corps to have armed conflict in the streets of Banja Luka. But then I would, as I do in the report, base how this particular situation was dealt with and in weeks -- literally weeks later in other areas in the Krajina, how it was dealt with differently. But you also had allegations and reports of armed groups blockading roads and -- in Prijedor, for example. So -- but I would concede your point, Mr. Ackerman, that it may well not have been in the interest of the 5th Corps to have armed activities in the streets of Banja Luka against a Serbian paramilitary group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's go now to a completely different matter, page 25, paragraph 1.42. You -- you cite the Court there to a speech given by Karadzic. And in that speech, he says, talking about the strategic goals of the Serbian people: "The first such goal is separation from the other two national communities, separation of states." He's talking there about trying to basically create separate states, which I suggest to you is fully in accord with the directions received from the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina in the plebiscite, where they voted to remain within Yugoslavia and not support an independent Bosnia and Herzegovina. Isn't that true? Isn't that just a reflection of what the plebiscite called for?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: I have not looked at the details of the plebiscite. My report doesn't cut to that. So I think for me to make any comments on whether that -- that is the case would -- would be somewhat -- somewhat difficult. All I can say is what he says in his speech. Clearly he believes that there should be a separation of states in Bosnia. But I don't believe that that statement and others through the 16th Assembly session simply meant that Bosnia was going to be divided into -- into state parts. And as I argued in my direct testimony, including highlighting some of the references from the 16th Assembly session, that internally within the -- or a component of that separation was going to involve the resettlement of populations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It wasn't just Karadzic that was talking about that. Various international conferences were talking about that. Cutilheiro was talking about that, Vance Owen were talking about that, the cantonisation of Bosnia and Herzegovina was a possible way to settle the issue there that was internationally favoured at some point. Isn't that true? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes, that's true, within the confines of an independent Bosnia and Herzegovina, of course but, you're right, the Cutilheiro plan and these plans were about the cantonisation and some agreement whereby Bosnia could be -- could be governed and managed with an element of -- with the agreement of the national parties within it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the concept of cantonisation certainly carried with it the -- the thought, the possibility that it would involve movements of population from canton to canton, Serbs into Serb areas, Muslims into Muslim areas, Croats into Croat areas, and so forth, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: I don't necessarily agree that cantonisation in itself means the movement of populations between -- between places, and I would be surprised that the Cutilheiro Plan was a plan to -- to allow for the movements of persons between cantons. I'm not sure that's the case. I would -- I'm not an expert on the Cutilheiro Plan, and I would have to -- to defer to others who may know more, but I would not -- I'd be surprise if the Cutilheiro Plan was an agreement that would allow for all these movements, as you say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, it certainly wouldn't be an agreement to prevent people from moving. Freedom of movement is an important humanitarian concept, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes, it is. But I'm thinking more along the lines of moving people out to somehow shape cantons or resettlement or whatever. But again, I'm not an expert on the Cutilheiro Plan, so I would defer to someone who is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is -- and you know that during the war in Croatia and in parts of Bosnia many, many Serbs became refugees, were uprooted from their homes, and went elsewhere, don't you?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes. And a significant number did come to the Krajina area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after four years of war and some horrendous things that happened during those four years, Bosnia-Herzegovina basically wound up being divided in the way that was in many ways suggest by Karadzic and by some of the international plans in the first place, so we now have a -- a Serb area, the Republika Srpska; the Muslim-Croat area, the Federation, and there have been significant population movements back and forth between the two, haven't there?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm not -- I think we're kind of straying away from the direct and anything really of relevance to what we should be talking about today.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Any time the witness feels like he's not capable of answering my questions, I'll move on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's not what my point was, but we're --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I take note of your objection, Mr. Nicholls, but I will allow the question and I'll see if the witness is prepared to answer it or not. It is relevant to the basic part of his report, in any case. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can I just read the question, Your Honour, again?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, clearly there are some areas that you could draw a similarity between what Karadzic said in 1992 and earlier and after four years of war. War was ended by the Dayton Agreement. The Dayton Agreement established two entities in Bosnia-Herzegovina, it -- within the borders of an independent Bosnia-Herzegovina. The Dayton Accord allowed for the movement back of displaced refugees, people who had been moved from their homes or who'd -- who'd left. So I'm not sure that after four years of war it's exactly as Karadzic planned, but clearly Bosnia as an independent state now has two entities, the Republika Srpska and the Federation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's move to something different, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm wondering if you want to take a break now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We can have a break now. Twenty-five minutes. Thank you. Mr. Ackerman, do I take it that in spite of the fact that we lost half an hour this morning this shouldn't make any difference?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We'll certainly finish within the time allotted, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I thank you, Mr. Ackerman. Twenty-five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, what we were talking about before we broke was the 16th session of the assembly of the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina held on 12 May 1992 and some things that persons appearing there had to say. I want to now direct your attention to paragraph 1.45 of that report where you talk about the speech of General Lieutenant-Colonel Mladic at that session. You quote him as saying: "People and peoples are not pawns, nor are they keys in one's pocket that can be shifted from here and there. It is something easily said but difficult to achieve. We cannot cleanse, nor can we have a sieve to sift so that the only Serbs would stay, or that the Serbs would fall through and the rest leave. I do not know how Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Karadzic would explain this to the world. People, that would be genocide. That does not mean that Muslims have to be expelled or drowned." That's language from his speech, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes, those are references from the translation speech that we have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then if we go on to what -- paragraph 1.46, you say this: "Even these comments should be placed in some context. As one of those expected to implement the goals, he may well simply have been more aware of the practical limitations of what the assembly were proposing, more wary of what conflict would actually entail, and potentially saw it from a soldiers' perspective that it was better to have the Muslims and Croats under control in territory rather than as he himself stated, "in the trenches fighting against us." Now, my understanding of what you're saying there is that the concern was that if Muslims and Croats leave what they were designing as Serb areas, and there was a war, that they would wind up being combatants fighting for the other side. I mean, that was his concern [Realtime transcript read in error "certain], wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: That was one of his concerns. Yes, I think he in particular listened to the Muslims, I feel, because he was quite focussed on the Croats as being an enemy. But one of, I think, his concerns was that it may well have been easier to control them if they were in a position of authority and control rather than, as he said, coming back to fight them later. So it was one of his concerns.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that there were efforts -- let's see, what have we got here? Line 29 -- line 7 on page 29, the word "certain" is actually "concern" was the word that was used there. Let me see if I can get back to where I was now. Once the war did break out, the other side of that situation also occurred, that was where Serbs wanting to leave Muslim areas and come into the Serb areas were prohibited from leaving. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll come to that later. It's actually in some documents that you've cited in your report. And we'll get to it later on in this cross. We'll find that. If we look at paragraph 1.49, please, you're talking again about separation of communities, being one of the strategic objectives for the Serbs. And then you talk about some of the other goals. You speak of -- down near the end much of the discussion related to this involved commentary on the mapping of territory, the acceptance of the stated Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. borders, the designation of land as Serb, and the control of that territory. Included in these discussions were references to seizing land not designated as Serb, but which may have been useful to trade at a later date. This practice was eventually integrated into later military directives. And even caused difficulties within 1st Krajina Corps units when territory was captured with the later indication that it may well have to be handed back as part of political negotiations. And the document that you cite for that proposition, that latter proposition, is Exhibit P1747, which I'd like you to take a look at. Your Honour, I think I can safely direct you to page 2, paragraph 5, "state of security and morale," I think that's section you were referring to. Please feel free to look at the entire report if you wish, but I think this is the part you cited us to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No objection to counsel pointing the witness to a particular section, but I'd also ask the witness be allowed to review the entire document if he so wishes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, you're correct, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I said that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think it is an issue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, yes, that is, I think, the reference.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Or the section within the reference.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, this is one of those items that's under the morale part of the report. In this case, it's both security and morale. With regard to morale, it says that the morale in the units has been declining because salaries have not been paid and families were not supplied with food, fuel, and other items. Then it talks about conscripts disapproving of the statement made by the President after the conference in London, that the army will give back 20 per cent of the liberated territories that their comrades have died for, and apparently makes them wonder whether further combat operations in Jajce and Gradacac are justified. I take it that you agree that's the section you were referring to; right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes, I haven't gone over the whole document, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're free to go over the whole document for yourself, and if you have any further comments you'd like to make, please go ahead. Take your time, Mr. Brown.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. No, I think that's the section, Mr. Ackerman --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I take it it's highly unlikely that whoever wrote that report actually spoke with every conscript in the VRS, but just kind of drew the conclusion that there were conscripts who were disapproving of the concept of giving back some of the liberated territories in a settlement. Correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Well, clearly the author of the document was the staff of the corps headquarters and undoubtedly would not have been able to speak to the thousands of soldiers within the corps. But it was the function of whoever would have compiled that section of the report, either in this case the security officer or the morale officer. That was his job. His job was to be informed of what was happening within the corps and to pass that information up to the higher command. I would also just point out that the actual comment is justifiably disapproved, presuming whoever wrote that section and General Talic as the signator of the document believed this also, was something that they disapproved of. So -- but to answer your question, you're right, it would be unlikely that the author would have spoken to every single conscript. But clearly it was their job to know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what you have probably there is a consensus that conscripts are disapproving of that and they are wondering whether further operations are justified. You translate that in your conclusion into that having caused difficulties within the corps. I don't see in there anywhere where it says that it caused difficulties within the corps.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: You're right, it doesn't say difficulties. But what you have here is a reference at a time when the 5th Corps were actively involved in operations against Jajce and in other areas, you have a reference here that conscripts and potentially the corps themselves, being the phrase "justifiably disapproved," are unhappy or appear unhappy with the statements of the SRBH president about having to hand back territory that they themselves had fought for. So to be completely accurate, it doesn't say difficulty itself, but the fact that it's talking about a morale problem in this respect and the fact that it's being flagged up to the VRS Main Staff would give me the impression that it was an issue or a difficulty or a problem that the corps wanted to raise to their superior command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It just seems to me if you were wanting to be honest with the Chamber and report your conclusion honestly to the Chamber, wouldn't it have been honest to say that it even caused grumbling within the conscripts of the 1st Krajina Corps, or maybe putting the word "justified" in there somewhere because that is in the report. But you deliberately chose the words that it caused difficulties, which I think says something different than what the report says, don't you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, from Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Again, I'm sorry, but I think he's answered this question. I think the witness said that when troops are questioning further combat operations and are dissatisfied, that's a difficulty. So I think he's answered this question of why he wrote that section, and obviously it is a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it's a case of res ipsa loquitur here. The contents of the report speak for themselves. I don't think we need to elaborate. Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Beginning at paragraph 1.50 on page 27, you begin to talk about the corridor, what is sometimes called the Posavina Corridor connecting the Krajina basically to Serbia. This was a road, for instance, a road link that would have connected Banja Luka to Belgrade if it had been open, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes. Amongst other things, I think Karadzic himself articulated why that area was important. It wasn't simply that it was a road link, but he said that the control of that area was important because it enabled Serb areas in Bosnia to be connected. It also enabled those areas to be connected with the Serb areas in Croatia, and it enabled those two areas to be connected with Belgrade. But yes, there was a road link. I actually believe there were two road links, but there was a road through that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And before the beginning of hostilities, the road was open and normal travel and trade could occur between Belgrade and the Krajina, for instance. Correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes, until it was severed or control was taken of some key municipalities by Croat units in, I believe, March 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you refer to that actually on page 133 of your report, paragraph 2.197. In April and May 1992, Croat forces took control of Derventa and Modrica severing the corridor road that ran through to Bijeljina and on to Serbia. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And the Croat forces closed that as a strategic goal, to cut off the supply line between Serbia and the Krajina, not just military supplies but civilian supplies also. It had strategic military importance, not just political importance, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: I haven't looked at the Croat operational directives, but clearly it had significant effect of the severance of that line. It did affect civilian supplies and military supplies, so I would agree it was -- it was of significant military importance to the Croats, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you look at page 28 of your report, it's paragraph 1.50, you actually quote something General Talic said about this in an order Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. apparently. General Talic said: "Motivate all units and armed structures in opening the road routes towards the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia by stressing the importance of control over the relevant areas in terms of the provision of supplies, the survival of the Serbs in the Bosnian Krajina, and the Serbian Republic of Krajina, the possibility of supplying the 1st and 2nd Krajina Corps, and of opening towards the world in general." So it was certainly recognised by General Talic and Karadzic and all of the persons involved that this was a key issue, not just militarily, but for the survival in terms of civilian supplies and so forth. Right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes, both General Talic and Karadzic clearly viewed this as a significant area. And hence the reason presumably that Karadzic placed it as strategic goal number 2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And of course with the war going on in Croatia, the previous supply lines between the Bosnian Krajina and, say, Zagreb and Croatia, for instance, also had stopped to function, and so by cutting off that corridor, the -- all trade into Croatia and into Serbia had been severed, hadn't it?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: I wouldn't necessarily say that all trade. There clearly was an air bridge to a certain degree, certain point. Troops were able to be flown in and out of Banja Luka I believe up until the point that an air embargo was imposed. And there are references clearly to black marketeering and smuggling and activities that were going on, if you like unofficially to, to get materials in and out. But you're right, clearly the severance of the corridor was also of some significance in terms of receiving supplies from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like you to look now at Exhibit P50, P5-0. This is the -- basically the transcript of that May 12th session that we have been talking about, of the 16th session of the Assembly of the Serbian People. And beginning at page 36 is this speech that was given by General Mladic. Unfortunately, I can't find the exact phrase that I wanted to refer you to because the document that I have is not the one I marked. So I'll come back to this later. I'll go on to something else. Look at P629, please. Now, what I've given you is a regular combat report dated 2 May of 1992. It's still the 5th Corps of the JNA, not the VRS. Correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In paragraph 3, the report is talking about the situation on the ground. It says this: "In the territory of our zone of responsibility, there have been no developments or incidents likely to seriously affect the combat readiness of the units. Caution, fear, and uncertainty are still present among the population of all nationalities. It is particularly prominent in crisis municipalities such as Prijedor, Bosanski Novi, Sanski Most, Bosanska Krupa, Bugojno, Gornji Vakuf, Donji Vakuf, and Jajce." If you go now to paragraph 6, again, we're talking about the morale section of the report. "Troops and officers are dissatisfied and angry with the acting Federal Secretary for National Defence, Colonel General Blagoje Adzic who visited Banja Luka but failed to state what will happen to the JNA in BH or how the issues related to the status of officers and civilian employees who are not from Serbia and Montenegro will be resolved -- whose army will we become and which state will be supporting the families of our fallen comrades and the disabled war veterans, since the official BH authorities have appealed to people not to go to war." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In paragraph 1.75 of your report, that would be on page 36, about halfway through that paragraph, you refer to this visit of Colonel General Blagoje Adzic to Banja Luka as being significant. How was it significant? What is it about that visit that you found and reported to be significant?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Well, it's significant because of who the man is. I mean, he's the most senior JNA officer at the time visiting -- visiting Banja Luka at a time of some uncertainty within the JNA, bearing in mind the issue of the new FRY constitution which had been announced a number of days prior to that. And what happened subsequently, which was the VRS was established a week or so later, Mladic was appointed as the commander of the VRS army. So I think it's significant in terms of who he is and why he comes to Banja Luka at a time of some interest. I think I referenced that visit somewhere else in the report as well, I believe. I have to go and check my footnotes, but I don't think this is the only time I mention it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, we're still talking about the JNA at this point. And Adzic was the secretary for National Defence. You think there's something significant when the secretary of National Defence visits a corps-level military structure?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You think that's unusual?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: I think it's significant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Do you think he visited other corps?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: I don't know if he visited other corps. I would imagine he visited the second military district, or potentially visited the second military district, but I don't know if he visited the other corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I want to ask you about what we just read there in paragraph 6 of this document: "... since the official BH authorities have appealed to people not to go to war." Do you know what that refers to?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: I don't. I can only speculate, but I don't know exactly what it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I want you to take a look now at another document. It's DB266. And also in connection with that, look at paragraph 1.75, which you should have in front of you.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Would you like me to put it on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's find the right place, first. If you look at 1.75, you have a sentence which begins: "An SFRY official instruction on the transformation of the JNA which kept Bosnian members of the army in positions within Bosnia and Herzegovina and sent Bosnians from serving in other republics back to Bosnia and Herzegovina was issued on 5 May 1992 and was probably the next official step in the process." Footnote 113. In that footnote, you refer to the document which you now have before you, 03028203 which is now Defence Exhibit 266. I don't believe that document says what you report that it says in paragraph 1.75, does it?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Which bits are you particularly referring to, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You pretty much have to refer to the entire document because the entire documents speaks -- I mean, it's only one paragraph long basically. What you told us was -- well, you can see what you told us there in 1.75 that this document says.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: It references a SFRY decision, presidency decision, on the transformation of the JNA. That's the phrase in the document. It's dated the 5th of May, which I've stated in the sentence. And those JNA members who -- or Bosnian -- who were in Bosnia are to remain there. And those who don't have Bosnian citizenship can remain if they want to; or if they express a desire to leave, to go back to the FRY, they should do so by the 10th of May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the document actually gave these people a choice, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Well, it gives a choice to those who are not BH citizens.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: That they could either stay if they wanted to, or if they express a desire, they can leave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what your report says is that it sent all these people from other republics -- maybe I'm reading this wrong.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: I think -- I remember writing this sentence on this document. I had to rewrite it a few times. I think the document also calls for those people who are Bosnian citizens but are not in Bosnia, so Serbia, Montenegro, and others, to go, to be sent to Bosnia. I think that's what I've written in my line here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So -- now, this is, of course, an instruction from the Federal Secretariat of National Defence of the JNA, Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. That's clear, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what's trying to be accomplished here is basically a reorganisation within the JNA inside Bosnia-Herzegovina, I think probably in connection with a resolution of the United Nations that ordered Milosevic to get the JNA out of Bosnia-Herzegovina basically. Correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Well, I'm not necessarily sure of that. I'd have to go and look at other material. I can only go on the face value of the document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the other thing we know from the document is that it is issued by an assistant commander for moral guidance and legal affairs, a Colonel Mesud Hasotic who I'm quite certain is a Muslim. Correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go now to the next page where you talk about mobilisation in your report. Now I want you to look again at the document we were looking at earlier, that P50, the minutes of that assembly. And with any luck, I'll be able to find the section I want to refer to. If you'll check, what's here is a speech by Mr. Brdjanin, I believe. You say in paragraph 1.77: "General mobilisation throughout the SRBiH as had been argued by General Lieutenant-Colonel Mladic, Radoslav Brdjanin and others in the 16th assembly session was announced on the 21st of May 1992 after a decision taken by the Presidency the previous day." The part is actually the second paragraph on that page where Brdjanin says this: "As for the military options, I do not know much about that, but I propose, as Mr. Zupljanin has said, that Serbian BH cannot be defended if it is based on the voluntary principle. If we establish Serbian armed forces today, we will be announcing general mobilisation, and now everyone must be put under the command of the Serbian armed forces and forces for preserving law and order." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: I don't see it on the ELMO, I think we're looking at a slightly different section.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think we're on page 31. Is that right, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's the page I'm on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You never said which page you were on, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Page 31, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you find what I was referring to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The paragraph starts with the words "as for the military options..."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And your question, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us in the -- in your report that general mobilisation was announced on the 21st May. You said: "As had been argued by Mladic, Brdjanin, and others in the 16th assembly, the impression one gets from reading that, I think, is that Brdjanin had called for a mobilisation." If you look at what he says, he just says that: "If we establish a Serbian armed forces today, we will be announcing mobilisation." Is there a difference there or not?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Maybe if you pick over the word "argued" possibly. If I look at the transcript now of what is said, it would almost indicate that Mr. Brdjanin had an awareness that mobilisation was going to be announced, which it was on the 20th of May, rather than just saying we should mobilise. It almost indicates here that the decision has been taken, and it will be announced at a later date, which of course it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And look what else he said right after that. He says: "All paramilitary units must truly disappear. Any private armies will only bring us harm and divide us." Right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know from other documents that that was a position that he maintained throughout the year of 1992, that he was throughout the year concerned about paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: I don't know. But I know that that type of comment was -- wasn't just Mr. Brdjanin making that comment. There were others, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And we got more to talk about with regard to that as we go on, too, so we'll get there. It's clear that what he says there about paramilitary formations, he's talking about Serb paramilitary formations, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's go now to paragraph 1.86 of your report. In that connection, I'd also like you to look at Defence Exhibit DB267. If you look at page 3 of that document, it speaks of military activity and what has been called the -- talk about the corridor that we have been talking about. Correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes, some of those areas are in the corridor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it's that corridor that we talked about just a few moments ago linking the Krajina area of Bosnia with Serbia. Correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it says -- that report indicates that the corridor once opened had been closed as a result of military activity and the withdrawal of the Tuzla Corps. And then it mentioned the SRJ. Do you know what the SRJ is?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: I think it's referring to the FRY, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honours, just for the record, this document is also P2514.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nicholls. 267, page 3. Yes, what's your next question, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm working on it, Your Honour. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to move on to another matter. I think I've asked all I want to ask about that. 1.103. We're under a heading called "cooperation with civilian bodies" on page 44. And in paragraph 1.103 you speak of Serb Crisis Staffs being established by the SDS from late 1991 in various municipalities. In your last sentence, you say this: "This coordination function" -- I better go back a little earlier. "It is evident that the Crisis Staffs were become an important form of organisation in ensuring that the resources of the municipality or the region were coordinated and unified in achieving the overall political and military objectives. To do this, they brought together the relevant civilians, military, and police bodies in a formalised grouping. This coordination function was the primary role of these bodies." Correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we look then at the next paragraph, you speak of a speech that was made by Karadzic on 27 March 1992. And in relation to the military, Karadzic said this: "You must try to organise the people so that they can defend themselves. Find a number of reserve officers for those staffs and have them register everyone who owns a weapon as well as units. They should organise Territorial Defence, and if the JNA is there, they must be placed under its command." So he's talking about taking these TO units and putting them under the command of the JNA, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this is a significant period of time prior to the creation of the VRS, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: I don't think it's a significant period of time. The VRS was created on the 12th of May, and this instruction -- this speech, I think was in late March. So I don't think that's a --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I'll withdraw the significant part. It was before the creation of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it smacks of an effort to achieve and continue some kind of a unified command to avoid competing commands, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes, I think Karadzic seems to be saying that in those areas where they need to defend themselves, they need to have this unified military command clearly indicating that the Territorial Defence and the JNA seem to have some shared, shared view. But you're right, it would seem to say this was would avoid any difficulties in that respect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Within any kind of military organisation a unified command is pretty important to being able to efficiently carry out whatever mission it is that the command is trying to carry out, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's go now to the next paragraph: In that paragraph, you refer to Document P157, and I think it would be helpful for you to have that exhibit in front of you as we speak about it. Now, this is a document dated April 26th of 1992, I believe, signed by Prime Minister Branko Dzeric of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina government. Correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you quote rather large parts of that in your report, presumably because you find this document particularly significant. Correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes, I think it's an important document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The first thing that I think is important about this document is that it makes it clear in paragraph 4 that Crisis Staffs are not to interfere with the operations of the TO or the police. Correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You then quote the section in paragraph 8 that provides that the Crisis Staff has the obligation to provide working and living conditions for JNA members. Right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, that paragraph certainly doesn't imply any kind of control by the Crisis Staffs over the JNA, does it?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: No, it doesn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It simply details to a limited extent that cooperation between civilian and military authorities that you referred to earlier in your report.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes, it's another example of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that paragraph talks about providing working and living conditions for JNA. If you look at the next paragraph, it uses almost the same language: "Shall provide working conditions for international peace and relief organisations. Doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And again that certainly wouldn't imply that the Crisis Staff was to have authority over international peace and relief organisations, does it?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, keep that document, and look also at P1265. P1265 is a decision on the organisation and operation of the Crisis Staff of the Prijedor Municipality. And I think you've pointed out in your report, and you'll see it in this document, that it's pretty clear that this document was created in response to the Dzeric document on instructions for the work of municipal Crisis Staffs because it contains the same language in many places, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So at least we can conclude that with regard to Prijedor Municipality, the instructions of Dzeric were implemented and had some significant as far as they were concerned?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes, it would appear so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Article 2 of that document, 1265, it talks about creating conditions for the Executive Board to exercise executive authority. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That seems to be an indication that while the Crisis Staff replaces the assembly of the municipality, the executive authority remains with the Executive Board, and the Crisis Staff has to create conditions so that they can exercise that executive authority. Correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: I'll just read your question, Mr. Ackerman, on the... Well, it would seem -- I can only go by what is written on the instruction, that the Crisis Staff is to create conditions for the Executive Committee to exercise legitimate executive power. What it says on the document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's move forward. I'm finished with that, now. 1.109 on page 47, you tell us this. You're talking about 5th Corps deployment to Western Slavonia, and the time when some of those units were returning. You say: "As these units were redeployed into municipalities, they were ordered to establish links with the local authorities. And it is that they were being redeployed back from Western Slavonia, from the fighting in Croatia, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes, certain units. I think the reference here was one was -- had been deployed in Western Slavonia and was being redeployed back to Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just so that we fully understand this situation, what had happened was when the war broke out in Croatia, units that were stationed in various localities in Bosnia-Herzegovina were mobilised and went into Croatia to join in the fighting there. And then when that was winding down, they came back to those areas in Bosnia and Herzegovina where they had been deployed from. Right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes, there were some units that were redeployed to other areas in the corps, not necessarily their home area. But most units went back to the areas that they had been deployed -- had come from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you say that they were ordered to establish links with local authorities upon their redeployment. There's nothing militarily unusual about this, is there? It's important, isn't it, for military units to try to maintain good relations with civilian authorities in the places where they're stationed?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes, and it was also contained in the regulations of the JNA. So no, it wasn't necessarily something that was unusual.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just for an example, let's look at P608. And this is a document you referred us to, I think, in paragraph 1.109 to.
